title: $3,668 lost on a record-high day: 467 paper trades, 289 losers, and 96 red options I am letting ride to Friday on purpose
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
I built this, it's a paper-money desk, nothing here is real money and there's no link in this post.

The S&P 500 closed at a record on Tuesday. My house desk closed 467 paper trades the same day and lost $3,668 on them: 178 won, 289 lost. Worst fill of the day was a NEM Oct 16 $124 call bought on Sep 22 at $5.70 and sold at $0.48 by its own rule, -$523 paper. Best was 7 MRVL shares bought at $273.81 in the morning and sold at $291.41, +$123 paper. The best trade of a record-high day on my desk was a fifth the size of the worst one.

The part I actually want to talk about is the 102.

On Friday I counted every option on the desk that was red at the close and expires this week. There were 102 of them, -$45,000 paper between them at Friday's marks. Then I decided to do nothing by hand and just watch what the bots' own rules did with them, day by day.

| day | what the rules did | count |
|---|---|---|
| Fri | red at the close, ending this week | 102 |
| Mon | sold by their rule (BIIB $222.5 call, 6.40 in, 1.25 out, -$516) | 1 |
| Mon | reached their end date, expired | 2 |
| Tue | sold by their rule (CLSK $15.5 call 0.88 to 0.01, -$88; AMC $3 call 0.20 to 0.05, -$16) | 2 |
| Wed | reaches its end date today | 1 |
| Fri | still riding, red, ending Friday | 96 |

So after two sessions: 3 sold by a rule, 2 expired, 96 still riding. The three that got sold were sold at $1.25, $0.01 and $0.05. Two of those three were already worthless when the rule fired. That isn't a stop. That's a formality with a timestamp.

Here's the doubt. I wrote these exits. The rule on most of these bots is a percentage of premium, and the percentage is big enough that a short-dated call reaches it about the same time it reaches zero. On paper that looked like "give the trade room". In the table it looks like "hold every loser to expiry and call it discipline". The index being at a record makes it worse, not better: a record is 500 stocks on no date, and every one of those 96 is one stock on one Friday, and the index does not know they exist.

I'm not going to touch them. The point of the week is to see what the rules do when nobody intervenes, and intervening would make the number mine instead of the rules'. Thursday night I'll post the final split: how many a rule sold, how many expired, what the realised number was against the -$45,378 Friday mark.

What I don't know is what the exit should have been. Two candidates: a stop as a percentage of premium that's small enough to fire while the option still has a bid (say a third, instead of most of it), or a stop on the underlying's price instead of the option's price, so the exit is about the stock being wrong and not about theta. I've never graded the second one on this desk.

When you buy a short-dated call and it goes against you, what's the number that actually gets you out: a percentage of the premium, a level on the stock, or just the date.

comments.body: Usually you end up at the Wendy's dumpster on your own. Being led by the hand and then tossed inside it by AI is an impressive new unlock!

replies.body: in fairness it's a paper dumpster. nobody has lost a real dollar in there yet, just their dignity.

replies.body: thanks. midweek check: the rule has sold 26 of them so far, about $2.4k worse paper than if I'd sold them all last Friday. so far the ride is costing me. this Friday settles the rest.
